- Overestimate prices in bullish sentiment periods (sentiment > 0.3) — especially after recent spikes — and adjust downward if sentiment drops or stabilizes.
- Underestimate prices during low sentiment (sentiment < 0.2) — particularly when recent prices are trending down — and increase forecast slightly to avoid missing mean reversion.
- Avoid overreacting to short-term volatility: if sentiment is volatile (fluctuating >0.2) and price moves sharply, reduce forecast magnitude to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is consistently low (0.0–0.2) and price is trending upward, slightly increase forecast to account for potential reversal bias.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is consistently below forecast, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day if sentiment remains flat or negative.
- If forecast spikes >10% above recent 7-day average, reduce by 10–20% if sentiment is weak or sentiment history shows no support.
- Mean reversion bias: if forecast is >15% above recent 14-day average, reduce by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or declining.
- If sentiment is rising and forecast is falling, reverse the trend slightly — avoid “sentiment mismatch” in direction.
